The Weilüe, a Chinese text composed in the early third century CE, describes the Roman Empire (Da Qin) as a vast kingdom located west of Parthia and the Great Sea, accessible by sea from Egypt in as little as two months with favorable winds [S1]. According to this source, the Roman Empire "has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns" and "extends several thousand li in all directions," with its capital city built with stone walls near the mouth of a river [S1]. A later Chinese historical record, the Hou Hanshu, documents that in 166 CE the king of Da Qin sent envoys bearing elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn, and turtle shell, though the Chinese compiler noted that "the tribute brought was neither precious nor rare, raising suspicion that the accounts [of the 'envoys'] might be exaggerated" [S3]. These Chinese sources thus portrayed Rome as a distant, powerful, and geographically extensive state, though they expressed skepticism about the value of goods presented in early diplomatic contact [S1][S3].
